title: Sustainable Development, SDGs and Green Economy

cards.h: The big idea behind all environment policy
cards.b:
Sustainable development is asked in Prelims through dates and conferences and in Mains through trade-off questions: growth versus environment, equity across generations.

The Brundtland definition and the SDG basics are must-knows.

Questions come in three forms. Prelims asks about a conference or report with year and place. Mains asks for a trade-off, such as whether growth and environment can go together. Essay topics use ideas such as intergenerational equity. A good opening is the Brundtland definition, followed by the three pillars and one Indian example.

The World Commission on Environment and Development, chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland, released Our Common Future in 1987. It defined sustainable development as development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

Three pillars: economic, social and environmental. Intergenerational equity and intragenerational equity are the core ideas.

Brundtland stressed the needs of the world's poor and the limits set by technology and social organisation. The report led to the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. Critics call the concept vague and say it lets growth continue. Weak sustainability allows natural capital to be replaced by manufactured capital, while strong sustainability does not.

• Stockholm 1972: first UN conference on the human environment; UNEP created.
  • Brundtland 1987.
  • Rio 1992 (Earth Summit): Agenda 21, Rio Declaration, UNFCCC, CBD, forest principles.
  • Johannesburg 2002: World Summit on Sustainable Development.
  • Rio+20 2012: “The Future We Want”; agreed to build SDGs and promote green economy.

The 17 Sustainable Development Goals with 169 targets were adopted by the UN General Assembly in September 2015 and run to 2030. They replaced the Millennium Development Goals (2000–15, eight goals).

SDGs apply to all countries, are indivisible, and include environment goals: 6 (water), 7 (energy), 11 (cities), 12 (consumption and production), 13 (climate), 14 (life below water) and 15 (life on land).

Planetary boundaries (Rockström and others, 2009) give safe limits for nine Earth systems. Doughnut economics (Kate Raworth, 2017) seeks a safe and just space between social floor and ecological ceiling. The Environmental Kuznets Curve claims pollution first rises with income, then falls, but evidence is mixed.

Weak sustainability allows manmade capital to replace nature; strong sustainability says natural capital cannot be fully replaced. Ecological footprint and green GDP are measures.

UNEP’s 2008 Green Economy Initiative defines a green economy as one that improves wellbeing and equity while reducing environmental risk. It includes renewable energy, circular economy, green jobs and nature-based solutions.

Critics say “green growth” hides continued resource use, and that poor countries need room to grow (degrowth debate).

India’s negotiating line at Rio and since is common but differentiated responsibilities: rich countries caused most historic emissions and must lead. Rio Principle 7 gives this its basis.

At home, Article 48A and 51A(g), along with the Environment Protection Act 1986, give the legal base. India’s Voluntary National Reviews report SDG progress to the UN.

Developing countries argue that development is the first need and that rich countries must lead. Others say the poor suffer most from degradation. The idea of just transition tries to link both.

The question also divides carbon prices, subsidies and trade rules.

The Environmental Kuznets Curve idea holds that pollution rises with income and then falls, but critics say this is not automatic. Developing countries point to the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, since rich countries emitted more in the past. Just transition means that workers and regions that depend on coal or other polluting activity are supported, not abandoned, when policy changes.

NITI Aayog publishes the SDG India Index. Its 2023–24 edition (released 2025) reported a national composite score of about 71, up from 66 in 2020–21 (as of 2025). Schemes such as GOBARdhan (2018), Jal Jeevan Mission, Ujjwala and Swachh Bharat map onto goals.

India’s Green Growth is one of the seven priorities of Budget 2023–24. India’s Mission LiFE and the 2070 net-zero target tie in.

The SDG India Index ranks states and Union Territories using indicators on poverty, health and clean energy, and Kerala has often ranked among the top states. It supports cooperative federalism by making states compete. The National Indicator Framework is run by MoSPI, and localisation of SDGs takes goals down to panchayats.

Mains-style: “Sustainable development is a balancing act. Examine how India can balance growth and environment.” Structure: definition; three pillars; Indian pressures (poverty, energy, population); tools (EIA, renewables, SDG localisation, green finance); conclusion with equity.

Prelims tip: Brundtland 1987. SDGs 2015: 17 goals, 169 targets. Agenda 21 from Rio 1992. UNEP created after Stockholm 1972.
